A verified authority record guarantees that the machine resolves command contention deterministically in silicon and code. But verifying that the nervous system switches authority according to specification does not guarantee that the resulting physical vehicle dynamics remain stable under real-world tarmac friction, worn actuators, and split-second driver reflexes. A handover that executes flawlessly at the bus protocol level can still induce dynamic rollover or road departure if the physical machine and the human operator are pushed beyond their combined operational limits.
<!-- END -->

## Systems Stress-Tests {#sec-intervention-14-9}

<!-- SECTION 14.9 -->
<!-- claim: A handover that succeeds mechanically and fails operationally. -->
<!-- covers: Stress-test 1: The Incapacitated Operator — a handover request issued to a distracted or incapacitated human who fails to respond before $T_{\text{timeout}}$, testing autonomous fallback to minimum-risk maneuver. -->
<!-- covers: Stress-test 2: Destructive Panic Override — an operator seizing manual control and commanding a violent maneuver directly into a physical obstacle, verifying that the nervous system barrier filter refuses the command. -->
<!-- covers: Stress-test 3: Babbling Field Bus — high-frequency spoofed takeover requests flooding the CAN bus, testing cryptographic authentication throughput and real-time command rejection without stalling the control loop. -->
<!-- covers: Stress-test 4: Cascading Retraining Degradation — injecting uncurated human intervention logs into a simulated 10-generation continuous training pipeline to measure the rate of policy capability collapse. -->

<!-- BEGIN -->
A handover that succeeds mechanically can still fail operationally. When the nervous system switches authority registers without bus errors, dropped packets, or torque deadlocks, the physical machine and its human operator may still enter unrecoverable failure modes if the timing, physical dynamics, adversarial communication loads, or downstream data pipelines violate the assumptions of the control architecture. The following four stress-tests examine where clean algorithmic and protocol-level handovers break down in physical execution, defining the failure boundaries that must be defended before an intervention architecture can be certified.

#### Stress-Test 1: The Incapacitated Operator (Handover Timeout and Fallback Maneuver) {.unnumbered}

**The Scenario.** An autonomous electric transport platform with a mass of $2400\text{ kg}$ operates in a mixed-traffic logistics facility at a constant forward velocity of $v = 15.0\text{ m/s}$ ($54.0\text{ km/h}$). The perception pipeline encounters localized optical steam and particulate occlusion, dropping state estimation confidence below the minimum threshold for autonomous navigation and issuing a structured handover request to the human safety operator at $t = 0\text{ s}$. The architecture allocates an operator reaction budget $T_{\text{react}} = 1.50\text{ s}$ and an unacknowledged timeout limit $T_{\text{timeout}} = 2.00\text{ s}$. The human operator is distracted or incapacitated, registering zero steering wheel torque ($|\tau_{\text{manual}}| < 0.2\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$) and applying no brake pressure. The physical clearance to a stationary steel barrier directly ahead is $42.0\text{ m}$.

**The Systems Dilemma.** While waiting for operator acknowledgment, the vehicle continues moving along its unguided path for $2.00\text{ s}$, traversing a displacement of $d_{\text{wait}} = v \times T_{\text{timeout}} = 15.0\text{ m/s} \times 2.00\text{ s} = 30.0\text{ m}$. At $t = T_{\text{timeout}}$, the nervous system detects the unacknowledged handshake and triggers its autonomous minimum-risk fallback maneuver, applying maximum emergency mechanical braking on dry concrete with an effective tire-road friction coefficient $\mu = 0.70$, yielding a deceleration of $a_{\text{brake}} = \mu g = 0.70 \times 9.81\text{ m/s}^2 = 6.87\text{ m/s}^2$. The required kinematic stopping distance from $15.0\text{ m/s}$ is $d_{\text{stop}} = v^2 / (2 a_{\text{brake}}) = (15.0)^2 / (2 \times 6.87) = 16.38\text{ m}$. Because the remaining physical clearance is only $42.0\text{ m} - 30.0\text{ m} = 12.0\text{ m}$, the vehicle collides with the barrier at a residual velocity of $v_{\text{impact}} = \sqrt{v^2 - 2 a_{\text{brake}} d_{\text{remain}}} = \sqrt{225 - 2 \times 6.87 \times 12.0} = 7.75\text{ m/s}$. Analyze this sequence and derive the dynamic relationship required between instantaneous obstacle clearance, current velocity, and $T_{\text{timeout}}$ to guarantee that fallback braking begins before the remaining clearance drops below $d_{\text{stop}}$.

**What a Good Answer Establishes.** The response must derive the compound stopping distance as a function of handover response budgets and physical deceleration limits, demonstrating why static handover timeouts create deterministic collision hazards when clearance shrinks. It must formulate an adaptive handover protocol where $T_{\text{timeout}}$ is dynamically constrained by the physical stopping margin, defending either progressive pre-braking during the handshake interval or early termination of the waiting window.

**The Physical AI Insight.** Handover is an allocation of physical distance rather than digital time. If the duration allocated for a human response exceeds the spatial stopping budget of the remaining clearance, the handshake protocol guarantees an impact before the timeout timer expires.

#### Stress-Test 2: Destructive Panic Override (Operator Overriding into an Obstacle) {.unnumbered}

**The Scenario.** A $350\text{ kg}$ autonomous mobile delivery robot travels along an access corridor at $v = 4.0\text{ m/s}$. A pedestrian steps from a blind doorway into the path at a range of $6.0\text{ m}$. An onboard or remote human operator panics, seizes manual steering authority with an aggressive manual torque input of $\tau_{\text{driver}} = 18.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$, exceeding the takeover threshold $\tau_{\text{override}} = 4.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$, and commands a hard lateral steering angle of $\delta = 35.0^\circ$ directly toward a plate-glass structural partition $2.5\text{ m}$ away. The preemption arbiter transfers full lateral steering authority ($\alpha = 1.0$) to the human within $T_{\text{handshake}} = 20\text{ ms}$.

**The Systems Dilemma.** The operator's command evades the pedestrian but places the vehicle on an unavoidable collision trajectory with a rigid physical boundary that will be reached in less than $650\text{ ms}$. The nervous system runs a deterministic Control Barrier Function filter on an isolated real-time microcontroller at $1000\text{ Hz}$, evaluating kinematic keep-out sets $h(\mathbf{x}) \ge 0$. If the architecture grants absolute priority to manual human commands, the machine executes the operator's input and impacts the glass partition. If the safety enforcer unilaterally clamps the actuator steering angle to satisfy $h(\mathbf{x}) \ge 0$, the resulting torque opposition between the human driver and the steering assist motor generates rapid limit-cycle oscillations on the column. Analyze the authority arbitration architecture and specify the mathematical constraint-projection mechanism required to prevent structural collision while preserving operator control along the unconstrained tangent of the safe set boundary.

**What a Good Answer Establishes.** The response must formulate the mathematical boundary where human manual commands are treated as unprivileged proposals subject to deterministic barrier enforcement rather than direct writes to actuator registers. It must derive the minimum-norm projection of the manual input vector onto the half-space of admissible control inputs, proving that the enforcer maintains physical safety invariants without inducing high-frequency mechanical fighting or instability on the steering linkage.

**The Physical AI Insight.** Taking control does not suspend physical invariants. Manual intervention grants authority to select among safe trajectories, never the authority to command a machine outside its physical survival envelope.

#### Stress-Test 3: Babbling Field Bus (Flooding the Authentication Channel) {.unnumbered}

**The Scenario.** A heavy mobile manipulator ($m = 4500\text{ kg}$) coordinates its chassis and arm drives over a Controller Area Network with Flexible Data-Rate (CAN-FD) bus operating at $5.0\text{ Mbps}$. The safety enforcer executes on an isolated ARM Cortex-R5 real-time core, evaluating invariant envelopes and refreshing actuator output registers every $1.00\text{ ms}$ ($1000\text{ Hz}$). Manual takeover frames require cryptographic authentication via a $64\text{-bit}$ message authentication tag (AES-128-GMAC) verified by an onboard hardware cryptographic accelerator requiring $18.5\text{ }\mu\text{s}$ per operation. A malfunctioning telemetry radio or babbling diagnostic node on the bus begins broadcasting invalid, spoofed takeover frames at a rate of $8000\text{ frames/s}$.

**The Systems Dilemma.** Each incoming frame triggers a receive interrupt on the real-time core, incurring $45.0\text{ }\mu\text{s}$ of interrupt service overhead, followed by an accelerator call consuming $18.5\text{ }\mu\text{s}$ to reject the invalid tag. At an ingress rate of $8000\text{ frames/s}$, processing these bogus packets consumes $(45.0\text{ }\mu\text{s} + 18.5\text{ }\mu\text{s}) \times 8000\text{ s}^{-1} = 508\text{ ms}$ of compute time every second ($50.8\%$ CPU utilization). This unexpected processing load and bus contention causes the $P_{99.9}$ loop execution time of the $1000\text{ Hz}$ safety task to expand from $620\text{ }\mu\text{s}$ to $1380\text{ }\mu\text{s}$. The real-time task misses consecutive deadlines, trips the hardware watchdog, and forces an uncommanded emergency actuator stop on an active transport lane. Evaluate this communication bottleneck and design a layered hardware acceptance filtering and rate-limiting architecture that rejects spoofed frames at the silicon controller interface without interrupting the main processor.

**What a Good Answer Establishes.** The response must construct an end-to-end timing budget accounting for bus serialization, peripheral interrupt latency, and cryptographic verification under peak adversarial traffic. It must specify hardware-level filtering mechanisms, including hardware mailbox acceptance masks and silicon token-bucket rate limiters, that drop unauthenticated packets before CPU interrupt assertion, proving that loop execution jitter remains within the $1.00\text{ ms}$ real-time budget.

**The Physical AI Insight.** Cryptographic authentication is a physical workload that consumes silicon cycles and bus bandwidth. A security mechanism that lacks hardware-level traffic policing defends against unauthorized takeovers by creating a real-time availability failure.

#### Stress-Test 4: Cascading Retraining Degradation (Dataset Poisoning via Uncurated Interventions) {.unnumbered}

**The Scenario.** A fleet of autonomous yard tractors records multi-sensor telemetry and intervention logs across $500{,}000\text{ hours}$ of depot operations. During this deployment, human safety drivers intervene $4200\text{ times}$ to take manual steering and throttle control. An automated continuous learning pipeline ingests these operational logs, extracts the $30\text{-second}$ trajectory segments preceding each takeover, and incorporates them directly into the imitation learning corpus for policy fine-tuning. The retrained policy is deployed in a closed-loop simulation across ten sequential training generations without manual human annotation or causal boundary filtering.

**The Systems Dilemma.** Human operators intervene for diverse operational reasons, where only $38\%$ of events represent true policy boundary failures, $44\%$ represent cautious early takeovers during nominal policy behavior, and $18\%$ represent driver error or accidental control taps. Furthermore, during the $3.0\text{ s}$ to $5.0\text{ s}$ reaction interval immediately preceding an intervention, operator situational awareness decays, leading to erratic micro-steering, hesitation, and inconsistent brake taps. By generation 4 of continuous retraining, the policy learns to reproduce these pre-takeover human hesitations in nominal lanes, causing phantom steering twitches. By generation 8, the policy exhibits severe distribution collapse, increasing the required intervention rate by $340\%$ and rendering autonomous operation unstable. Formulate an automated data curation pipeline that separates true corrective actions from human noise and pre-intervention policy degradation.

**What a Good Answer Establishes.** The response must analyze the causal mechanics of policy degradation from uncurated intervention logs, showing why treating pre-takeover telemetry as expert demonstration corrupts the state-action distribution. It must specify an automated segmentation protocol that truncates the pre-takeover reaction window ($T_{\text{react}}$) from the training set, extracts only the stable post-takeover recovery trajectory where $\alpha = 1.0$, and conditions policy updates strictly on verified physical state improvements.

**The Physical AI Insight.** Interventions are not expert demonstrations. Training a policy on raw takeover logs teaches the model to imitate the human hesitation, delayed reflexes, and physical instability that precipitated the intervention.
<!-- END -->

## Summary {#sec-intervention-14-10}

<!-- SECTION 14.10 -->
<!-- claim: Chapter 12 receives a system whose authority is defined. -->
<!-- covers: Human authority is an engineered real-time interface with explicit operational scope, cryptographic identity, and timing bounds, not an informal safety net. -->
<!-- covers: Bumpless transfer requires continuous actuator blending bounded by plant jerk limits to prevent driveline shock and loss of physical stability. -->
<!-- covers: Operational intervention data requires cryptographic tamper-evidence for post-incident liability and rigorous causal truncation to prevent retraining bias. -->
<!-- covers: The Authority Record provides Chapter 15 with explicit fault-injection targets and Chapter 16 with the foundational evidence for human-machine safety claims. -->

<!-- BEGIN -->
Human authority over a moving machine cannot function as an informal safety net or an unmodeled override switch. Authority is an engineered real-time interface defined by explicit operational scope, cryptographic identity, and deterministic timing bounds. While enforcement in Chapter 12 provides the reflex mechanisms that refuse an unsafe model action, intervention addresses the complementary problem of acquiring authority and revoking the autonomy of an executing policy. When an operator touches a steering yoke, depresses an emergency pedal, or issues an override command across an authenticated network link, the nervous system must arbitrate that request within strict timing deadlines before the physical state diverges. Consider an analytical example of a vehicle traveling at $15.0\text{ m/s}$ ($54\text{ km/h}$). If the nervous system requires $200\text{ ms}$ of round-trip bus negotiation to authenticate an operator token and resolve authority conflicts, the vehicle travels $3.0\text{ m}$ along an unmanaged trajectory before the takeover begins. Treating intervention as an external exception rather than an explicit state transition in the nervous system converts the takeover mechanism itself into an unbudgeted failure mode.

Transferring control away from an active policy is never an instantaneous step function. If an actuator abruptly swaps a learned policy's torque command for a human operator's raw input within a single $1\text{ ms}$ control cycle, the sudden force discontinuity induces driveline shock, wheel slip, and structural vibration. Bumpless transfer requires continuous actuator blending, where an authority parameter $\alpha(t)$ transitions smoothly from zero to one along a trajectory governed by the physical plant's maximum jerk limits. In an analytical example of a $2000\text{ kg}$ vehicle chassis with an actuator rate limit of $35\text{ Nm/s}$ and a lateral jerk bound of $2.5\text{ m/s}^3$, blending the learned policy and the human override across a $150\text{ ms}$ window prevents the transient torque spike that would otherwise break tire traction. The nervous system enforces these plant dynamics throughout the handover, guaranteeing that neither the policy's residual momentum nor the human operator's sudden counter-steering forces the physical plant beyond its envelope of dynamic stability.

Every intervention event generates operational telemetry that directly governs both post-incident liability analysis and model retraining. Because an intervention marks the exact boundary where autonomous control was revoked, the resulting logs require cryptographic tamper-evidence. Hardware security modules must sign the Authority Record at the bus level, writing timestamped hash chains to non-volatile storage to create an immutable log of arbitration decisions. In a post-incident forensic investigation, the absence of cryptographic integrity reduces engineering claims to unverified assertions. Signed telemetry provides the only empirical proof of whether a collision resulted from an unhandled model failure, a late enforcer trigger, or an erratic human override that forced an actuator into saturation.

For the machine learning training pipeline, raw intervention logs represent a severe hazard if ingested without causal filtering. Human operators do not intervene with the precision of optimal feedback controllers. During the $3.0\text{ s}$ to $5.0\text{ s}$ reaction window immediately preceding an intervention, human situational awareness decays, producing hesitation, inconsistent pedal taps, and erratic micro-steering inputs. Feeding these uncurated pre-takeover windows into an imitation learning pipeline corrupts the state-action distribution, training future model generations to replicate the very human instabilities that precipitated the failure. An automated data curation pipeline must apply causal truncation to discard the pre-intervention reaction window, isolating only the verified recovery trajectory where human authority reached full control and stabilized the physical state.

A physical AI system cannot be verified or certified until its authority boundaries are formalized. By defining human authority as a deterministic, cryptographically authenticated, and physically rate-limited interface, the Authority Record provides the concrete specifications required for verification and safety assurance. In Chapter 15, this record defines the explicit fault-injection targets needed to test whether the machine maintains physical stability under dropped override packets, delayed tokens, and actuator saturation. In Chapter 16, the tamper-evident records and bounded transfer guarantees supply the empirical evidence required to construct a defensible safety case. Without an engineered intervention interface, a physical AI system remains an unconstrained experimental prototype. With it, the machine possesses a verifiable boundary of control.
<!-- END -->
